God commanded a day of rest and worship from the beginning. Christians moved it to Sunday, the day Jesus rose.
A friendship that never meets in person fades. Weekly Mass keeps us close to Jesus and to his family, even when we do not feel like it.
The Church asks us to go every Sunday not to burden us, but because she knows we need it, the way a mother insists you eat.

sym2-03.think: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." A day set apart says: my time belongs to God first.
sym2-03.journal: What usually gets in the way of Sunday Mass for you? How could you make it easier?
sym2-03.pray: Lord, this is the day you have made. Let me rejoice and be glad in it.
sym2-03.do: Plan your Sunday now: which Mass time, how you will get there, and something restful for the afternoon.

sym2-03.title: Mass in the forests of Huronia

story.name: St. John de Brébeuf and the Canadian Martyrs
story.text:
John de Brébeuf was a French Jesuit who came to New France in 1625. He lived among the Wendat (Huron) people near Georgian Bay, in what is now Ontario, learned their language, wrote a dictionary, and composed the "Huron Carol" so they could sing of Jesus' birth in their own words.

At the mission of Sainte-Marie he and his companions celebrated Mass in a chapel of bark and wood. In 1649, during war, he was captured and tortured to death. He and seven companions are honoured as the patrons of Canada. You can visit the Martyrs' Shrine in Midland, Ontario.

sym2-03.think: Malachi foresaw that "in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation." The Mass was offered in Canada's forests long before its cathedrals.
sym2-03.journal: What does it mean to you that the same Mass is celebrated all over the world, every day?
sym2-03.pray: Holy Canadian Martyrs, pray for Canada, and for all who bring the Gospel in a new language.
sym2-03.do: Listen to the Huron Carol ("'Twas in the moon of wintertime"), and pray for the Indigenous peoples of Canada.

sym2-03.title: Prepare for Sunday
sym2-03.think: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." A little preparation makes Mass much richer.
sym2-03.journal: What will you offer to God at Mass this Sunday (a worry, a person, a thanks)?
sym2-03.pray: Lord, I am coming to your house. Prepare my heart to listen and to give.
sym2-03.do: Pray with Sunday's Gospel using Lectio Divina, and arrive ten minutes early to sit in silence.

sym2-03.title: Questions about the Mass
sym2-03.class: What do you still find confusing at Mass: when to stand or kneel, the words, the gestures, the colours, why the priest does something? Write it down.
sym2-03.think: "On the first day of the week, when we were assembled to break bread..." From the very beginning Christians gathered on Sunday for the Eucharist, even late into the night.
sym2-03.journal: What will you look for at Mass this Sunday that you never noticed before?
sym2-03.pray: Lord, thank you for the Mass, the greatest prayer of all. Teach me to love it.
sym2-03.do: Read your questions once more and bring them to class.

sym2-04.title: Peace be to you
sym2-04.think: On Easter night the risen Jesus breathes on the apostles and says, "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." The first gift of the Resurrection is forgiveness, given through people.
sym2-04.journal: What did you feel in class when you heard about Confession?
sym2-04.pray: Jesus, you came through locked doors to give peace. Come through the locked doors of my heart.
sym2-04.do: Read the first Confession preparation page in the app, just the first section.

sym2-04.title: The father ran
sym2-04.think: The son rehearses his speech of shame, but the father "running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." He does not let him finish. This is what Confession is like.
sym2-04.journal: What would you want to hear from the Father if you came home?
sym2-04.pray: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. Run to me, and bring me home.
sym2-04.do: Do this week's Bible study on the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32).

sym2-04.title: Why go to Confession?

media.title: Fr. Mike on Confession
media.about: Fr. Mike has many short videos on Confession: why we confess to a priest, what to do if you are nervous, what to say, and why it is "the sacrament of freedom." Pick the one that answers your biggest worry.
media.listen: what the priest is really thinking when he hears a confession.

sym2-04.think: "Because I was silent my bones grew old... I said: I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven." Hidden sin weighs; spoken sin is lifted.
sym2-04.journal: What is your biggest fear or question about Confession?
sym2-04.pray: Lord, I confess to you. Take the weight from my bones and give me joy again.
sym2-04.do: Write your fear about Confession in "My questions for class."

sym2-04.title: Why tell my sins to a priest?

reason.q: Why not confess directly to God?
steps: You can and should tell God you are sorry every day. But Jesus chose to give the power to forgive sins to his apostles, and he knew human nature.
We need to hear forgiveness, not only hope for it. In Confession you hear the words "I absolve you" with your own ears.
Sin hurts the whole Body of Christ, so reconciliation includes the Church. The priest stands in for Christ and for the community.
The priest can never reveal what he hears, under any circumstances (the "seal of confession"). Priests have gone to prison and even died rather than break it.

sym2-04.think: "Confess therefore your sins one to another... the continual prayer of a just man availeth much." Confessing aloud was part of Christian life from the start.
sym2-04.journal: How does it feel to know you will hear "you are forgiven" out loud?
sym2-04.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for the gift of Confession. Give me courage to use it.
sym2-04.do: Find out when your parish offers Confession, and note it in your calendar for when you are ready.

sym2-04.title: He knelt, and his life changed

story.name: St. Charles de Foucauld
story.text:
Charles de Foucauld was a rich French officer who lost his faith as a teenager and lived for pleasure. As an explorer in Morocco he was moved by the prayer of Muslims, and he began to ask, "My God, if you exist, let me know you."

In 1886, in a Paris church, he went to ask a priest, Abbé Huvelin, questions about faith. The priest told him, "Kneel down and make your confession." He did, then received Communion, and later wrote: "As soon as I believed there was a God, I knew I could do nothing else but live for him." He became a priest and lived as a hermit and brother to all among the Tuareg in the Sahara, where he was killed in 1916.

sym2-04.think: Charles came with intellectual questions and was invited to kneel first. Sometimes the answer to our questions begins with being forgiven.
sym2-04.journal: "My God, if you exist, let me know you." Write your own version of this prayer.
sym2-04.pray: Father, I abandon myself into your hands; do with me what you will. Whatever you may do, I thank you. (St. Charles de Foucauld)
sym2-04.do: Pray Charles's prayer of abandonment slowly, once in the morning and once at night.

sym2-04.title: Examine your day
sym2-04.think: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." A short daily look at your conscience keeps the heart soft and ready for Confession.
sym2-04.journal: Tonight: where did I love well today, and where did I fall short?
sym2-04.pray: I confess to almighty God and to you, my brothers and sisters, that I have greatly sinned.
sym2-04.do: Pray the Evening Examen tonight, five minutes before sleep.

sym2-04.title: Questions about healing
sym2-04.class: What do you want to ask about Confession or the Anointing of the Sick: how often, what counts as a sin, what to say, what if I forget something?
sym2-04.think: "They that are well have no need of a physician, but they that are sick." Jesus came for sinners, so there is a place for you.
sym2-04.journal: What would you like Jesus the physician to heal in you before Easter?
sym2-04.pray: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins.
sym2-04.do: Learn the Act of Contrition by heart this week, using practice mode.

sym2-05.title: Sacraments for others
sym2-05.think: Matrimony and Holy Orders are "sacraments at the service of communion": they are given mainly for the good of others. A husband and wife, and a priest, are signs of how Christ loves his Church.
sym2-05.journal: Whose marriage or priesthood has inspired you, and why?
sym2-05.pray: Lord, bless every marriage I know, and every priest who serves your people.
sym2-05.do: Pray today for one married couple and for your parish priest, by name.

sym2-05.title: The wedding at Cana
sym2-05.think: Jesus' first sign is at a wedding. He turns water into the best wine, more than anyone needed. He blesses marriage and promises that with him, the best is yet to come.
sym2-05.journal: Where has the "wine" run out in your life, or in a relationship?
sym2-05.pray: Mary, tell Jesus where the wine has run out. Jesus, I will do whatever you tell me.
sym2-05.do: Do this week's Bible study on Cana (John 2:1-11).

sym2-05.title: Marriage and vocation

media.title: Fr. Mike on marriage and vocation
media.about: Fr. Mike talks about vocation, God's call for each life, and about marriage as a covenant, not a contract: a promise to love "for better, for worse," which only makes sense with God's grace.
media.listen: the difference between a contract and a covenant.

sym2-05.think: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the church, and delivered himself up for it." The model for married love is the cross: a gift of self.
sym2-05.journal: What do you think God is calling you to in this season of life?
sym2-05.pray: Lord, show me my vocation, and give me a generous heart to follow it.
sym2-05.do: If you are married, do one small act of service for your spouse today. If not, for a family member.

sym2-05.title: Why marriage for life?

reason.q: Isn't a lifelong promise unrealistic today?
steps: Jesus raised the bar: what God has joined, let no man put asunder. He knew it was hard; that is why he made marriage a sacrament, with grace to live it.
Love that is only "for now" is not yet a full gift. Children, spouses and societies all flourish on promises that can be trusted.
The Church does not abandon people whose marriages failed. An annulment looks at whether a true marriage existed from the start, and divorced people are welcome at Mass.
If marriage is a picture of God's faithful love, then its permanence is not a cage but good news: God's love does not walk away.

sym2-05.think: When the disciples said this was hard, Jesus did not lower the ideal. He promised help to reach it.
sym2-05.journal: If you have questions about your own marriage situation for RCIA, write them privately here to ask your priest.
sym2-05.pray: Lord, heal every broken marriage and every wounded family, including mine.
sym2-05.do: If your marriage situation needs looking at before Easter, ask your RCIA coordinator this week. It is common and they can help.

sym2-05.title: A married couple, both saints

story.name: Sts. Louis and Zélie Martin
story.text:
Louis was a watchmaker and Zélie made fine Alençon lace in France in the 1800s. Both had wanted to enter religious life and were turned away. They met on a bridge, married in 1858, and had nine children; four died young, a deep grief they carried with faith.

They went to early Mass together each day, cared for the poor, and ran their businesses honestly. Zélie died of cancer at 45. Their youngest daughter became St. Thérèse of Lisieux, who said, "God gave me a father and mother more worthy of heaven than of earth." In 2015 they became the first married couple canonized together.

sym2-05.think: Holiness is not only for priests and nuns. Louis and Zélie became saints through work, children, grief and ordinary love.
sym2-05.journal: Where in your ordinary life could you become holy?
sym2-05.pray: Sts. Louis and Zélie, pray for families, for parents who grieve, and for my home.
sym2-05.do: Do your work today as a prayer: offer it to God before you start.

sym2-05.title: Pray for priests
sym2-05.think: A priest is "taken from among men" and "can have compassion on them that are ignorant and that err, because he himself also is compassed with infirmity." Priests are human, and need our prayer.
sym2-05.journal: What would you like to thank your parish priest for?
sym2-05.pray: Lord Jesus, High Priest, keep our priests close to your heart. Give them joy, courage and holiness.
sym2-05.do: Write a short thank-you note to your priest or catechist and give it to them this week.

sym2-05.title: Questions about vocations
sym2-05.class: What do you want to ask about marriage, priests, deacons, religious sisters and brothers, or your own situation? Write it down.
sym2-05.think: Young Samuel hears God call three times and doesn't recognize the voice. Eli teaches him to say, "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth."
sym2-05.journal: Who is your "Eli", someone who helps you recognize God's voice?
sym2-05.pray: Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.
sym2-05.do: Read your questions once more, and thank your sponsor for walking with you.

sym2-06.title: The way to happiness
sym2-06.think: Jesus begins his great sermon with "Blessed", meaning happy. Catholic morality is not first about rules; it is about the happiness God made us for, and the way that leads there.
sym2-06.journal: Which of the Beatitudes surprises you most? Why?
sym2-06.pray: Jesus, teach me the way of the Beatitudes. Make me poor in spirit, meek and merciful.
sym2-06.do: Choose one Beatitude and live it on purpose today.

sym2-06.title: The Ten Commandments
sym2-06.think: God gave the commandments after he freed Israel from slavery: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out." They are the rules of freedom, so that we never become slaves again, to sin, to things or to ourselves.
sym2-06.journal: Which commandment do you find hardest to live?
sym2-06.pray: Lord, your law is perfect, reviving the soul. Write it on my heart.
sym2-06.do: Do this week's Bible study on the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:1-12).

sym2-06.title: Freedom for excellence

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on freedom
media.about: Bishop Barron often contrasts two ideas of freedom: "freedom of indifference" (doing whatever I want) and "freedom for excellence" (being able to do what is truly good, like a pianist free to play Chopin after years of practice). God's law trains us for the second.
media.listen: the example of learning a language or an instrument.

sym2-06.think: "You, brethren, have been called unto liberty: only make not liberty an occasion to the flesh, but by charity of the spirit serve one another." Freedom is for love.
sym2-06.journal: Where do you feel unfree, stuck in a habit you wish you could change?
sym2-06.pray: Lord, set me free, not to do whatever I want, but to become who you made me to be.
sym2-06.do: Pick one small habit to practise this week (prayer, patience, honesty) and track it in My weekly habits.

sym2-06.title: Who decides what is right?

reason.q: Isn't morality just personal opinion?
steps: If right and wrong were only opinion, then "cruelty to children is wrong" would be no truer than "I prefer tea." Almost no one really believes that.
Every culture shares a core moral law: honour parents, do not murder, do not steal, keep promises. Paul says it is "written in their hearts."
A real moral law points to a real Lawgiver. Our conscience is like a voice that comes from beyond us.
The Church's moral teaching is not a list of arbitrary bans. It explains what helps human beings flourish, and offers mercy when we fail.

sym2-06.think: Even people who never read the Bible know, deep down, that some things are truly good and others truly evil. That knowledge is a gift from God.
sym2-06.journal: When has your conscience told you clearly what was right?
sym2-06.pray: Holy Spirit, form my conscience in truth. Give me the courage to follow it.
sym2-06.do: Read the Catechism paragraphs on conscience (1776-1782), or the summary in your lesson.

sym2-06.title: Verso l'alto: to the heights

story.name: St. Pier Giorgio Frassati
story.text:
Pier Giorgio was born in 1901 to a rich and powerful family in Turin, Italy. He loved mountain climbing, jokes and his friends. He also went to Mass daily, gave away his bus fare and walked home so he could give money to the poor, and spent hours in the slums caring for the sick.

At 24 he caught polio, probably from someone he was helping, and died within a week. His family was astonished when thousands of poor people filled the streets for his funeral; they had no idea what he had been doing. He used to write "Verso l'alto", "to the heights", on his mountain photos.

sym2-06.think: Micah sums up the moral life: "to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." Pier Giorgio did all three, with joy.
sym2-06.journal: What is one hidden good you could do this week that nobody will know about?
sym2-06.pray: St. Pier Giorgio, pray for me, that I may climb toward the heights with joy.
sym2-06.do: Do one secret act of generosity today, and tell no one.

sym2-06.title: If you love me, keep my commandments
sym2-06.think: Jesus links love and obedience: "If you love me, keep my commandments." It is like keeping a promise to someone you love: not a burden, but a way of saying "you matter to me."
sym2-06.journal: Which commandment could you keep today as an act of love for Jesus?
sym2-06.pray: O my God, I love you above all things, with my whole heart and soul, because you are all good and worthy of all love.
sym2-06.do: Keep one commandment today with special care: honesty in every word, or patience at home.

sym2-06.title: Questions about the moral life
sym2-06.class: What moral questions do you have: about conscience, specific sins, how strict the Church is, or a hard situation? Write them down.
sym2-06.think: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life." God does not force us; he invites us to choose life.
sym2-06.journal: What would choosing life look like for you this week?
sym2-06.pray: Lord, I choose life. Help me to love you, obey your voice and hold fast to you.
sym2-06.do: Read your questions once more before class.

sym2-07.title: Charity is patient
sym2-07.think: Real love is not mainly a feeling. Paul describes it with verbs: patient, kind, not envious, not proud, bearing all things. Love is willing the good of the other, and it comes from God who is love.
sym2-07.journal: Put your own name in place of "charity" in these verses. Which line is hardest to read?
sym2-07.pray: Lord, you are love. Make my love patient and kind, not proud or self-seeking.
sym2-07.do: Practise one line of 1 Corinthians 13 today with someone difficult.

sym2-07.title: The greatest of these
sym2-07.think: "Charity never falleth away." Knowledge, prophecy and tongues will pass. Faith and hope will one day be fulfilled. Only love lasts into eternity, because God is love.
sym2-07.journal: What would you do differently if you believed only love lasts?
sym2-07.pray: Lord, let my life be built of the one thing that lasts: love.
sym2-07.do: Do this week's Bible study on 1 Corinthians 13.

sym2-07.title: Love is an ability

media.title: Love is an Ability
media.about: Fr. Mike explains that love is not just something that happens to us, like falling in love. It is an ability we can grow, like a muscle: the ability to choose another person's good, even when it costs us.
media.listen: how to "train" love in small daily choices.

sym2-07.think: "Let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Love is proved by what we do.
sym2-07.journal: Whom could you love "in deed" today, in one concrete way?
sym2-07.pray: Jesus, you laid down your life for us. Teach me to love in deed and in truth.
sym2-07.do: Do one concrete act of love today that costs you something: time, comfort or money.

sym2-07.title: Is love just a feeling?

reason.q: If love is a feeling, why does the Church make rules about it?
steps: Feelings are real and good, but they come and go. If love were only a feeling, no promise of love could ever be kept.
Love in the full sense is a decision to seek another's good. Jesus commands it ("love one another"), and you can only command what can be chosen.
Using someone for my pleasure or benefit, however good it feels, is the opposite of love. The Church's teaching protects people from being used.
The measure is Jesus: "as I have loved you." His love was faithful, generous, and gave everything.

sym2-07.think: "By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." Love is the Church's identity card.
sym2-07.journal: When have you seen love as a choice rather than a feeling?
sym2-07.pray: Lord, when I do not feel like loving, give me the grace to choose love anyway.
sym2-07.do: Choose to be kind to someone today when you don't feel like it.

sym2-07.title: A mother's choice

story.name: St. Gianna Beretta Molla
story.text:
Gianna was a doctor in Italy, a paediatrician who loved skiing, mountaineering, music and fashion. She married Pietro Molla in 1955 and they had three children. Her letters to him are full of tenderness.

In 1961, pregnant with their fourth child, she was found to have a tumour in her uterus. The doctors offered treatments that would save her but end the baby's life. She chose the surgery that protected her child, telling the doctors, "If you must choose between me and the child, do not hesitate: choose the child." Her daughter Gianna Emanuela was born healthy; Gianna died a week later. Her daughter became a doctor too.

sym2-07.think: Gianna loved life, her husband and her children, and that is exactly why she gave herself. Real love is not the absence of other loves but the gift of self.
sym2-07.journal: Who has given themselves for you? Write a line of thanks.
sym2-07.pray: St. Gianna, pray for mothers, for doctors, and for all families expecting a child.
sym2-07.do: Thank your mother, or someone who was like a mother to you, today.

sym2-07.title: Love your neighbour as yourself
sym2-07.think: The lawyer asks, "who is my neighbour?" Jesus tells a story and turns the question around: be a neighbour to whoever needs you.
sym2-07.journal: Who is the "wounded traveller" in your life right now?
sym2-07.pray: Lord, open my eyes to see the people I usually pass by, and give me a heart that stops.
sym2-07.do: Stop for someone today you would normally pass by: a neighbour, a co-worker, a person asking for help.

sym2-07.title: Questions about love
sym2-07.class: What do you want to ask about love, friendship, dating, marriage, or loving difficult people? Write it down.
sym2-07.think: "Love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench charity." The Bible even contains a book of love poetry, because human love is a sign of God's.
sym2-07.journal: What did you learn about love this week?
sym2-07.pray: Set me as a seal upon your heart, Lord. Let nothing quench your love in me.
sym2-07.do: Read your questions once more before class.

sym2-08.title: Your body is a temple
sym2-08.think: "Your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost... For you are bought with a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body." The body is not a machine we own; it is a gift and part of who we are.
sym2-08.journal: What did you hear in class about the body and sexuality that was new to you?
sym2-08.pray: Holy Spirit, you live in me. Help me to honour my body and the bodies of others.
sym2-08.do: Take care of your body today as a gift from God: rest, eat well, take a walk.

sym2-08.title: Bone of my bones
sym2-08.think: "It is not good for man to be alone." God makes a partner equal to him, and the man sings for joy. "They shall be two in one flesh." Sexuality is part of the goodness of creation, made for love and life.
sym2-08.journal: What does it mean that we are made for communion, not for being alone?
sym2-08.pray: Creator, thank you for making us male and female, for love and for life. Heal what is wounded in me.
sym2-08.do: Do this week's Bible study on Genesis 2:18-25.

sym2-08.title: The Theology of the Body

media.title: Fr. Mike on the Theology of the Body
media.about: St. John Paul II taught that the body "speaks a language": it is made to say "I give myself to you, freely, totally, faithfully and fruitfully." Fr. Mike explains this in simple terms, with honesty about how hard it is in today's culture.
media.listen: the four words: free, total, faithful, fruitful.

sym2-08.think: Paul calls marriage "a great sacrament" because it points to Christ and the Church. Married love is meant to be an image of God's own love.
sym2-08.journal: Which of the four words (free, total, faithful, fruitful) speaks to you most?
sym2-08.pray: St. John Paul II, pray for us, that we may see our bodies and our love the way God does.
sym2-08.do: Be careful today with what you watch and scroll. Choose what honours people.

sym2-08.title: Why does the Church care what I do in private?

reason.q: Isn't sex a private matter between consenting adults?
steps: Sex is never only private: it involves another person, often creates a new person, and shapes families and societies.
Consent is necessary but not enough. Two people can freely agree to something that still hurts them. Love asks not only "Do you agree?" but "Is this truly good for you?"
The Church teaches that the body's language says "I give myself to you completely." Only a lifelong, faithful marriage open to life tells that truth with the body.
This teaching is demanding, and many struggle. The Church offers mercy, Confession and patience, never contempt.

sym2-08.think: "For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto sanctification." Holiness reaches every part of us, including the body.
sym2-08.journal: If you have questions or struggles here, write them honestly. They stay on your phone.
sym2-08.pray: Lord, purify my heart, my eyes and my desires. Where I have fallen, lift me up.
sym2-08.do: If something here weighs on you, plan to bring it to Confession or to a priest you trust.

sym2-08.title: A pope who loved human love

story.name: St. John Paul II
story.text:
Karol Wojtyła grew up in Poland. By 21 he had lost his mother, brother and father. He worked in a quarry under Nazi occupation and studied in secret to become a priest. As a young priest he went kayaking and hiking with groups of young couples and listened to their joys and struggles in love.

From those friendships came his writing on love, and later, as Pope, 129 talks known as the Theology of the Body. He taught that the human person "cannot fully find himself except through a sincere gift of himself." He visited Canada three times, including World Youth Day in Toronto in 2002.

sym2-08.think: "I will praise thee, for thou art fearfully magnified: wonderful are thy works." You were knit together by God. Your body is part of that wonder.
sym2-08.journal: What does "a sincere gift of self" look like in your life right now?
sym2-08.pray: Do not be afraid. Open wide the doors to Christ. (St. John Paul II) Lord, I open my doors to you.
sym2-08.do: Spend time with a friend today without your phone, giving them your full attention.

sym2-08.title: Blessed are the clean of heart
sym2-08.think: Jesus looks at the heart, not only at actions. Chastity is not repression; it is the freedom to love without using, to see people as persons, not objects.
sym2-08.journal: Where do you need God's help to see others with a clean heart?
sym2-08.pray: Lord, give me a clean heart, that I may see you, and see every person as you see them.
sym2-08.do: When a thought or image tempts you to use someone today, pray a Hail Mary for that person instead.

sym2-08.title: Questions about love and sexuality
sym2-08.class: This topic raises many questions: contraception, cohabitation, same-sex attraction, past relationships, your own situation. Write down what you want to ask, publicly or privately.
sym2-08.think: "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God... be reformed in the newness of your mind." God wants all of us: body, mind and heart.
sym2-08.journal: What did you learn this week that you want to remember?
sym2-08.pray: Lord, I offer you my body, my mind and my heart. Renew me.
sym2-08.do: If a question is private, ask to speak with your priest or catechist alone after class.

sym2-09.title: You did it to me
sym2-09.think: At the judgment Jesus says, "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Catholic social teaching starts here: Christ is hidden in the poor.
sym2-09.journal: Where have you met Christ in someone poor or in need?
sym2-09.pray: Lord Jesus, open my eyes to see you in the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner.
sym2-09.do: Learn the seven works of mercy for the body: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit prisoners, bury the dead.

sym2-09.title: Learn to do good
sym2-09.think: God tells his people that the fast he wants is to "deal thy bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the harbourless into thy house." Prayer without justice is incomplete.
sym2-09.journal: Who in your neighbourhood or city is most forgotten?
sym2-09.pray: Lord, let my light break forth like the dawn, by caring for those in need.
sym2-09.do: Do this week's Bible study on Matthew 25:31-46.

sym2-09.title: A civilization of love

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on Catholic social teaching
media.about: Bishop Barron explains the main principles of Catholic social teaching: the dignity of every person, the common good, solidarity, care for the poor, and subsidiarity (solving problems at the most local level possible). It is neither left nor right; it is the Gospel applied to society.
media.listen: why both the state and the family have their own roles.

sym2-09.think: The first Christians "had all things common... neither was there any one needy among them." Love became visible in how they shared.
sym2-09.journal: What do you have that you could share more freely?
sym2-09.pray: Lord, make me generous with what I have, because all of it comes from you.
sym2-09.do: Find out what your parish or the local Society of St. Vincent de Paul does for the poor.

sym2-09.title: Why does God allow poverty?

reason.q: If God is good, why doesn't he end poverty?
steps: The world produces enough food for everyone. Most hunger comes from war, greed, corruption and indifference: from human choices.
God's answer to poverty is not a miracle that removes our responsibility. It is a people: the Church, sent to feed, heal and share.
History shows it: Christians founded many of the first hospitals, orphanages, schools and food banks, including in Canada, where nuns founded the first hospitals in Quebec and Montreal.
So the question turns back to us, as John says: if we see a brother in need and close our heart, "how doth the charity of God abide in him?"

sym2-09.think: God has chosen to need us. Our hands are how he feeds his children today.
sym2-09.journal: What is one thing you could do this month about poverty near you?
sym2-09.pray: Lord, I cannot fix the world, but I can love one person. Show me who.
sym2-09.do: Put aside a little money or food this week for a food bank or someone in need.

sym2-09.title: Mother of the poor in Montreal

story.name: St. Marguerite d'Youville
story.text:
Marguerite was born in Quebec in 1701. Her husband was a fur trader who sold alcohol illegally to Indigenous people and left her deep in debt; he died after eight years of marriage, and four of their six children died young.

Instead of becoming bitter, she opened her home to the poor. People mocked her and called her group "les soeurs grises" (a pun meaning both "grey nuns" and "tipsy nuns", because of her husband). She kept the name. She took over Montreal's failing general hospital and cared for the sick, the old, abandoned babies and soldiers from both sides of the war. She was the first saint born in Canada.

sym2-09.think: Marguerite turned her own suffering into compassion. The insult became the name of a great work of love.
sym2-09.journal: How could a hurt in your life become a source of compassion for others?
sym2-09.pray: St. Marguerite d'Youville, pray for the poor of Canada, and for all who care for them.
sym2-09.do: Look up the Grey Nuns or a local shelter, and pray for the people they serve.

sym2-09.title: Care for our common home
sym2-09.think: God put the man in the garden "to dress it, and to keep it." Caring for creation is part of loving God and our neighbour, especially the poor, who suffer most when the earth is harmed.
sym2-09.journal: What in creation makes you most grateful to God?
sym2-09.pray: Praised be you, my Lord, for Brother Sun and Sister Moon, for Sister Water and Mother Earth. (St. Francis)
sym2-09.do: Do one thing today to waste less: food, water, plastic or electricity.

sym2-09.title: Questions about justice
sym2-09.class: What do you want to ask about Catholic social teaching, politics, money, work, immigration or the environment? Write it down.
sym2-09.think: "Let judgment run down as water, and justice as a mighty torrent." Amos says God is not impressed by worship that ignores the poor.
sym2-09.journal: How can your faith change the way you work, shop or vote?
sym2-09.pray: Lord, let justice roll down like waters, beginning in my own life.
sym2-09.do: Read your questions once more before class.

sym2-10.title: In the image of God
sym2-10.think: "God created man to his own image." Every human being, before birth or near death, rich or poor, healthy or disabled, citizen or refugee, carries that image. That is where dignity comes from.
sym2-10.journal: Whose dignity is easiest for you to forget?
sym2-10.pray: Lord, you made every person in your image. Help me to honour each one I meet today.
sym2-10.do: Greet everyone you meet today, including those people usually ignore.

sym2-10.title: Before I formed thee
sym2-10.think: "Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee." God knows and loves each person before birth. That is why the Church defends life from conception to natural death.
sym2-10.journal: What does it mean to you that God knew you before you were born?
sym2-10.pray: Lord, you knew me before I was born. Thank you for the gift of my life.
sym2-10.do: Do this week's Bible study on Genesis 1:26-31.

sym2-10.title: Every life is sacred

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on human dignity
media.about: Bishop Barron shows that the idea that every human being has equal dignity came into the world through the Bible. Ancient cultures did not believe it; it rests on the conviction that each person is made in God's image and loved by him.
media.listen: where our modern idea of human rights really comes from.

sym2-10.think: "What is man that thou art mindful of him?... Thou hast made him a little less than the angels." Small in the universe, yet crowned with glory.
sym2-10.journal: When have you felt small, and how does this psalm answer that?
sym2-10.pray: O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!
sym2-10.do: Look at the night sky tonight, and then at a face you love. Both are God's work.

sym2-10.title: Where do human rights come from?

reason.q: Why should every person have equal dignity?
steps: People are not equal in strength, intelligence, health or usefulness. If dignity depended on those, some people would be worth more than others.
If human beings are only the product of chance, it is hard to explain why a weak or unwanted person should have rights.
The Bible gives a reason: every person is made in God's image and loved by him. Our worth is given, not earned, so it cannot be taken away.
That is why the Church defends the unborn, the disabled, the dying, the migrant and the prisoner with the same voice. It is one principle, applied consistently.

sym2-10.think: "There is neither Jew nor Greek... bond nor free... male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus." In Christ, no one is worth less.
sym2-10.journal: Have you ever been treated as less than others? How does this teaching speak to you?
sym2-10.pray: Lord, you see no one as worthless. Give me your eyes.
sym2-10.do: Stand up, gently, for someone who is mocked or left out this week.

sym2-10.title: Something beautiful for God

story.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
story.text:
Agnes Bojaxhiu was born in 1910 in Skopje, of Albanian parents. She became a Loreto sister and taught girls in Calcutta for almost twenty years. On a train in 1946 she heard Jesus' call to serve "the poorest of the poor."

She left the convent with five rupees, wearing a simple white sari with blue stripes. She picked up the dying from the streets so they could die with dignity, loved. "Each one of them is Jesus in disguise," she said. Her Missionaries of Charity now serve on every continent, including in Canada. She also lived for decades in spiritual darkness, feeling nothing in prayer, and kept serving.

sym2-10.think: Mother Teresa did not wait to feel God before loving. She served Jesus in the poor even when prayer felt empty. Love was her prayer.
sym2-10.journal: Who is "Jesus in disguise" in your life this week?
sym2-10.pray: St. Teresa of Calcutta, pray for me, that I may do small things with great love.
sym2-10.do: Do one small thing today with great love, as Mother Teresa taught.

sym2-10.title: Welcome the stranger
sym2-10.think: "If a stranger dwell in your land... let him be among you as one of the same country: and you shall love him as yourselves: for you were strangers in the land of Egypt." Many of us, too, were newcomers once.
sym2-10.journal: When were you a stranger, and who welcomed you?
sym2-10.pray: Lord, you were a refugee in Egypt as a child. Bless every newcomer to Canada, and make me welcoming.
sym2-10.do: Reach out to a newcomer in your parish, neighbourhood or work this week.

sym2-10.title: Questions about life and dignity
sym2-10.class: What do you want to ask about abortion, euthanasia (MAID in Canada), the death penalty, war, racism or disability? Write it down. These are hard and important questions.
sym2-10.think: "Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Defending life is a choice we make again and again.
sym2-10.journal: What did you learn about human dignity this week?
sym2-10.pray: Lord of life, protect the weakest among us, and give me courage to speak for them.
sym2-10.do: Read your questions once more. This ends the second part of Symbolon, and Lent is coming.

s26.title: Return to me with all your heart
s26.think: "Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping... rend your hearts, and not your garments." Lent is forty days of coming home. For you, it is the last retreat before the sacraments.
s26.journal: What do you want God to change in you during this Lent?
s26.pray: Lord, I return to you with all my heart. You are gracious and merciful, slow to anger and rich in kindness.
s26.do: Choose your three Lenten practices: one for prayer, one for fasting, one for giving. Write them down.

s26.title: In secret
s26.think: Jesus names three practices: almsgiving, prayer and fasting, and says to do each one "in secret," for the Father who sees. Lent is not a show; it is a private conversation of love.
s26.journal: Which of the three is hardest for you, and why?
s26.pray: Father, you see in secret. Let my Lent be for you alone.
s26.do: Do this week's Bible study on Matthew 6:1-18.

s26.title: Why fast?

media.title: Fr. Mike on Lent and fasting
media.about: Fr. Mike explains why Catholics fast in Lent: not to earn God's love, but to make room for it. Saying no to small good things trains us to say no to bad ones, and hunger reminds us that we need God more than bread.
media.listen: how fasting and prayer work together.

s26.think: Jesus fasts forty days and is tempted. He answers each temptation with Scripture: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God."
s26.journal: What is your strongest temptation, and which word of God could answer it?
s26.pray: Lord Jesus, you were tempted as I am. Give me your strength when I am weak.
s26.do: In Canada, Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence, and Fridays of Lent are days of abstinence from meat. Plan yours.

s26.title: Does God care what I eat?

reason.q: If God looks at the heart, why do outward practices like fasting matter?
steps: We are body and soul, and they affect each other. What we do with the body shapes the heart, just as kneeling helps us pray.
Fasting is found in nearly every religion and was practised by Moses, Elijah and Jesus himself. It is a human way of saying "God comes first."
Isaiah warns that fasting without justice is empty. The Church joins the two: what we save by fasting is given to the poor.
The Church's rules are small and gentle (two fast days a year, meatless Fridays in Lent) so that everyone can join, and the sick, the young and the elderly are excused.

s26.think: "Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? loose the bands of wickedness... Deal thy bread to the hungry." The best fast changes how we treat others.
s26.journal: What could you give up this Lent that would help you love God and others more?
s26.pray: Lord, let my fasting free me, and let what I save feed someone hungry.
s26.do: Give up one thing today (a snack, a show, social media) and give the time or money to God or the poor.

s26.title: He kissed the leper

story.name: St. Francis of Assisi
story.text:
Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant in Assisi, Italy, a party-loving young man who dreamed of becoming a knight. He was horrified by lepers and would hold his nose and ride past them.

One day, riding near Assisi, he met a leper on the road. Something moved in him: he got off his horse, gave the man money and kissed his hand. "What had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body," he wrote. He gave up his wealth, lived in poverty, cared for lepers, and founded the Franciscans. He loved Lent so much that he kept several "Lents" each year.

s26.think: Jesus "having compassion on him, stretched forth his hand; and touching him" healed the leper. Lent asks us to touch what we avoid.
s26.journal: Who or what do you avoid, that God might be asking you to approach?
s26.pray: Lord, make me an instrument of your peace. Where there is hatred, let me sow love.
s26.do: Do one thing today you have been avoiding out of discomfort: a visit, a call, a kind word.

s26.title: Prayer, fasting, almsgiving
s26.think: "Prayer is good with fasting and alms, more than to lay up treasures of gold." The three Lenten practices belong together, like three legs of a stool.
s26.journal: How are your Lenten practices going so far? Be honest and gentle with yourself.
s26.pray: Lord, I am weak. Thank you for your mercy when I fail, and give me a fresh start.
s26.do: Pray the Stations of the Cross this Friday, at church or in the app.

s26.title: Questions about Lent
s26.class: What do you want to ask about Lent, fasting rules in Canada, the Rite of Election, or the coming weeks? Write it down.
s26.think: "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." Not someday. Now.
s26.journal: What is God saying to you "now," in this Lent?
s26.pray: Lord, now is the day of salvation. I do not want to wait any longer to give you my heart.
s26.do: Look at the rites ahead: how many days to the Easter Vigil?

s27.title: Heal what is weak
s27.think: On the third, fourth and fifth Sundays of Lent, the parish prays over the elect in the scrutinies, using three Gospels: the woman at the well, the man born blind and Lazarus. Each one is about Jesus healing and freeing.
s27.journal: What part of the scrutinies do you look forward to, or feel nervous about?
s27.pray: Jesus, you give living water. I am thirsty. Give me this water, that I may not thirst again.
s27.do: Drink a glass of water slowly today, and thank Jesus for the living water of Baptism.

s27.title: I was blind, now I see
s27.think: Jesus makes clay, anoints the blind man's eyes and sends him to wash. He comes back seeing. In the early Church, Baptism was called "enlightenment." This is what is about to happen to you.
s27.journal: What do you see now that you could not see a year ago?
s27.pray: Lord, open the eyes of my heart. One thing I know: that whereas I was blind, now I see.
s27.do: Do this week's Bible study on John 9.

s27.title: The man born blind

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on the man born blind
media.about: Bishop Barron's Lenten sermons on John 9 show how the healed man grows step by step, from "the man called Jesus" to "a prophet" to "Lord, I believe," while the religious experts, who think they see, become more and more blind.
media.listen: the three steps of the man's faith.

s27.think: The man is thrown out for telling the truth, and Jesus goes looking for him: "Dost thou believe in the Son of God?" "Lord, I believe."
s27.journal: Have you lost anything or anyone because of your faith journey?
s27.pray: Lord, I believe. Find me when others push me away.
s27.do: Write down your own three steps: who Jesus was to you at first, then, and now.

s27.title: Can people really change?

reason.q: Isn't it naive to think a sacrament can change who I am?
steps: We know from experience that people change, through love, suffering, friendship and choices. Change is part of being human.
Christianity adds that God himself acts in us. Baptism does not change our personality; it gives us a new relationship with God and a new power to grow.
Change is usually gradual, like the blind man's faith. The scrutinies pray against what holds us back and for what is good in us.
The lives of the saints, and of many ordinary converts, show real and lasting change. You can ask your sponsor about theirs.

s27.think: "If then any be in Christ a new creature, the old things are passed away, behold all things are made new."
s27.journal: What is one thing you hope will be made new in you?
s27.pray: Lord, make me a new creation. I give you the old things; make all things new.
s27.do: Ask your sponsor this week how faith has changed their life.

s27.title: Seven devils, then the first witness

story.name: St. Mary Magdalene
story.text:
Luke tells us Jesus had freed Mary of Magdala from "seven devils." We do not know exactly what she suffered, only that Jesus healed her completely, and that from then on she followed him and supported his work.

She stayed at the cross when most of the men ran away. On Easter morning she went to the tomb in the dark and wept when she found it empty. A man she thought was the gardener said one word, "Mary," and she knew him. Jesus sent her to tell the apostles. The Church calls her "the apostle to the apostles."

s27.think: Jesus called her by name, and she recognized him. The scrutinies are like that: God naming what binds us, and calling us by name into freedom.
s27.journal: What "devils" (fears, habits, wounds) do you want Jesus to drive out?
s27.pray: St. Mary Magdalene, pray for me, that I may hear Jesus call my name.
s27.do: Pray the prayer of deliverance before sleep: "Jesus, I give you what binds me. Set me free."

s27.title: Lazarus, come out
s27.think: Jesus says three things at Lazarus' tomb: "Take away the stone," "Lazarus, come forth," and "Loose him, and let him go." Others help remove the stone and the bandages. Community matters in conversion.
s27.journal: Who is helping to "unbind" you on this journey?
s27.pray: Lord, call me out of every tomb. Bless the people who help unbind me.
s27.do: Thank one person today who has helped you on your way to faith.

s27.title: Questions about the scrutinies
s27.class: What do you want to know about the scrutinies, the exorcism prayers, what to wear or do, or what your sponsor does? Write it down.
s27.think: "You were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord. Walk then as children of the light." An ancient baptism hymn: "Rise thou that sleepest, and Christ shall enlighten thee."
s27.journal: How have you changed since you started RCIA?
s27.pray: Christ, light of the world, shine on me. Wake me, raise me, and let me walk in your light.

s28.title: Believe in your heart, say it with your lips
s28.think: Paul says faith lives in two places: in the heart that believes and on the lips that confess. The Creed joins them. When you say "I believe," you are not reciting a list; you are giving yourself to the God it describes.
s28.journal: Which line of the Creed did you hear differently in class this week?
s28.pray: Lord, I believe. Let what I say with my lips live in my heart.
s28.do: Pray the Apostles' Creed slowly, stopping for a breath after each line.

s28.title: What I received, I handed on
s28.think: Here Paul writes down a short creed he had received himself, only a few years after Jesus died: Christ died for our sins, was buried, rose on the third day and appeared to many. The Creed you are learning grows from this same root.
s28.journal: Who handed the faith on to you? Write their names and thank God for them.
s28.pray: Thank you, Lord, for the long chain of believers who carried the faith all the way to me.

s28.title: What the Creed really says

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on the Creed
media.about: Bishop Barron walks through the Creed line by line. He shows that "I believe in one God" is a bold claim: it means nothing else, not money, not power, not pleasure, not success, gets to be God in my life. Each article is a door into the life of the Trinity.
media.listen: what the word "one" rules out in your life.

s28.think: Israel's oldest creed is "Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord." It was meant to be spoken at home, on the road, lying down and rising up. A creed is for everyday life, not only for church.
s28.journal: What competes with God for first place in your life?
s28.pray: You alone are God. I give you first place in my day.
s28.do: Start memorizing the Nicene Creed, the one we say at Sunday Mass. Learn the first part today.

s28.title: Aren't all religions the same?

reason.q: If every religion leads to God, why does it matter which Creed I say?
steps: Religions really do share a lot: prayer, a moral law, a longing for God. The Church respects whatever is true and holy in them (Vatican II).
But they also say different things, and the differences are not small. Was Jesus God or only a prophet? Did he die on the cross or not? Did he rise? These cannot all be true at once.
Saying "they are all the same" can sound respectful, but it ignores what each one actually believes. Taking a religion seriously means asking: is it true?

Christianity rests on a claim you can test: a man in history said "I am the way, the truth and the life" and then rose from the dead. If that happened, he is not one path among many; he is the one who makes every true path lead home.

s28.think: The Church teaches that people who do not know Christ through no fault of their own, but seek God sincerely, can be saved by his grace. Yet the fullness of truth is a gift too good to keep to ourselves.
s28.journal: What faith did you or your family grow up with? What good did you receive there?
s28.pray: Jesus, you are the way, the truth and the life. Lead all who seek God, my family too, to you.
s28.do: Pray today for someone you love who follows another religion or none.

s28.title: The brilliant mind who called his work straw

story.name: St. Thomas Aquinas
story.text:
Thomas was born in Italy around 1225 to a noble family who wanted him to become a powerful abbot. When he chose instead to join the Dominicans, a new order of poor preaching friars, his brothers kidnapped him and locked him in the family castle for more than a year. He spent the time praying and studying, and in the end they let him go.

He was big and quiet, and his classmates nicknamed him "the dumb ox." His teacher answered that this ox would one day bellow so loudly the whole world would hear. Thomas became one of the greatest thinkers in history, showing that faith and reason are friends. In Lent of 1273 he preached a series of sermons on the Apostles' Creed to ordinary people in Naples. A few months later, after an experience of God during Mass, he stopped writing. "Everything I have written seems like straw compared to what I have seen," he said. He died the next spring.

s28.think: The man who wrote thousands of pages about God ended in silent wonder. Studying the faith is good; meeting the God it speaks of is the goal.
s28.journal: Is your faith more in your head, or more in your heart, right now? What would help bring the two together?
s28.pray: Grant me, O Lord my God, a mind to know you, a heart to seek you, wisdom to find you. (from a prayer of St. Thomas Aquinas)
s28.do: Learn the next part of the Nicene Creed.

s28.title: A faith that walks
s28.think: James asks what good it is to say "I have faith" while a hungry neighbour is sent away. The Creed is not finished when we stop speaking; it continues in what we do.
s28.journal: Pick one line of the Creed. How could you live it today?
s28.pray: Lord, let my life say the Creed even when my lips are silent.
s28.do: Do one hidden act of kindness today as your "I believe."

s28.title: Ready to give the Creed back
s28.class: Which words of the Creed are still unclear to you? "Consubstantial," "descended into hell," "the communion of saints"? Write down the ones you want explained.
s28.think: Paul tells Timothy to guard the good thing entrusted to him, with the help of the Holy Spirit. The Creed is now being entrusted to you.
s28.journal: Write the Creed in your own words, as if explaining it to a friend.
s28.pray: Holy Spirit, help me to guard the faith and to hand it on.
s28.do: Try saying the whole Nicene Creed from memory.

s29.title: When you pray, say Father
s29.think: The first word is the most daring: Father. Jesus lets us call God by the name he himself uses. The whole prayer is the Gospel in a few lines: God's name, his kingdom, his will, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection.
s29.journal: Which line of the Our Father touches you most this week? Why?
s29.pray: Pray the Our Father very slowly, one phrase at a time.
s29.do: Pray the Our Father three times today: morning, noon and night.

s29.title: Lord, teach us to pray
s29.think: The disciples watched Jesus pray and wanted what he had. He gave them words, then a story about a friend who keeps knocking at midnight. God is not reluctant; he wants us to ask, seek and knock.
s29.journal: What do you want to ask God for, honestly, today?
s29.pray: Lord, teach me to pray. I knock, and I trust you will open.

s29.title: Our Father, line by line

media.title: Fr. Mike on the Our Father
media.about: Fr. Mike looks at why Jesus says "our" and not "my": we never pray alone. He explains "hallowed be thy name" (may your name be treated as holy), "thy kingdom come" (may your reign start in me), and why we ask for bread only for today.
media.listen: why it is "our" Father and "daily" bread.

s29.think: Paul says the Spirit makes us cry out "Abba, Father." Abba is the word a child uses at home. At Baptism you become a child of God, not in a poetic way, but truly.
s29.journal: What was your experience of a father? How does it help or hurt the way you see God?
s29.pray: Abba, Father, I am your child. Heal whatever makes it hard for me to trust you.
s29.do: Learn the Our Father by heart in the words used at Mass in Canada, if you have not yet.

s29.title: Why does God seem silent?

reason.q: I pray and feel nothing. Is anyone listening?
steps: Feelings are real, but they are not a measure of God's presence. You do not feel the earth spinning, yet it carries you every moment.

The Bible is honest about this. Psalm 13 begins "How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me?" Jesus himself prayed "My God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Feeling abandoned is part of the prayer of God's own people.
Many saints went through long dry times: Mother Teresa for about fifty years, Thérèse of Lisieux at the end of her life. They kept praying, and their love grew stronger, not weaker.
Prayer is not mainly about what we feel but about whom we turn to. Showing up when it is dry is a real act of love, like staying with a friend in a long silence.

s29.think: The psalm that starts with "How long?" ends with "I will sing to the Lord." Honest complaint and trust can live in the same prayer.
s29.journal: Write a short "How long, Lord?" prayer of your own. Then add one line of trust.
s29.pray: Lord, even when I feel nothing, I choose to stay with you.
s29.do: Pray for five minutes today, even if it feels empty. Just stay.

s29.title: A little way to God

story.name: St. Thérèse of Lisieux
story.text:
Thérèse Martin was born in France in 1873. Her mother died when she was four, and she grew up sensitive and easily in tears. At fifteen she wanted to enter a Carmelite convent so badly that she asked Pope Leo XIII in person for permission. She entered, and died there of tuberculosis at twenty-four.

She never did anything famous. She called her path "the little way": doing small things with great love, trusting God like a child trusts a parent. When she was too tired or dry to pray, she wrote, she would say an Our Father very slowly, and that was enough. In her last eighteen months she lived through deep darkness against faith, and kept making acts of trust. Her short autobiography, The Story of a Soul, has been read by millions. She is now a Doctor of the Church.

s29.think: Jesus says unless we become like little children we will not enter the kingdom. Thérèse shows what that means: not childish, but trusting, small and full of love.
s29.journal: What small thing could you do today with great love?
s29.pray: For me, prayer is a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven. (St. Thérèse) Lord, I look to you.
s29.do: Do one small, unseen task today, just for God.

s29.title: As we forgive
s29.think: The Our Father has one line with a condition: forgive us as we forgive. Peter asks if seven times is enough. Jesus says seventy times seven: forgiveness without counting.
s29.journal: Is there someone you find hard to forgive? You can write their initial only.
s29.pray: Lord, I am not ready to feel forgiveness, but I choose it. Help my heart to follow.
s29.do: Pray an Our Father for the person you find hardest to forgive.

s29.title: Good gifts from the Father
s29.class: What do you want to ask about prayer? How to pray when distracted, what to say, how long, whether memorized prayers count? Write it down.
s29.think: If we know how to give good gifts to our children, how much more will the Father give good things to those who ask him.
s29.journal: How has your prayer changed since you started RCIA?
s29.pray: Father, I trust you to give me what is truly good.
s29.do: Read your questions once more before class.

s30.title: Hosanna to the Son of David
s30.think: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, not a war horse. The crowd shouts Hosanna; in a few days a crowd will shout "Crucify him." Holy Week asks which voice is mine.
s30.journal: What did you learn in class about the days ahead? What are you looking forward to, and what makes you nervous?
s30.pray: Hosanna, Lord Jesus. Come into my city, my home and my heart.
s30.do: Find out the times of the Holy Week services at your parish and put them in your calendar.

s30.title: He loved them to the end
s30.think: On Holy Thursday Jesus kneels and washes his disciples' feet, the job of a servant. Then he gives them the Eucharist. Both say the same thing: I give myself to you completely.
s30.journal: Where is Jesus asking you to serve in a humble way?
s30.pray: Lord, wash me, and teach me to wash the feet of others.

s30.title: Walk the Way of the Cross

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: The Stations of the Cross with Bishop Barron
media.about: A guided prayer through the fourteen Stations of the Cross, from Jesus condemned to death to his burial in the tomb. At each station Bishop Barron offers a short reflection and a prayer. You can watch it in pieces, a few stations at a time.
media.listen: one station that stays with you. Come back to it on Good Friday.

s30.think: Seven centuries before Jesus, Isaiah describes a servant "wounded for our iniquities" who goes silent like a lamb to the slaughter. The early Christians read this and saw Jesus.
s30.journal: Which station of the cross speaks to your own life right now?
s30.pray: We adore you, O Christ, and we bless you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world.
s30.do: Pray the Stations of the Cross, in the app or at your church.

s30.title: Why did Jesus have to die?

reason.q: If God can do anything, why not just forgive us without the cross?
steps: Sin is not only breaking a rule; it is breaking a relationship and damaging the world. Real forgiveness does not pretend the damage is not there.
On the cross we see what sin does: the best person who ever lived is betrayed, mocked and killed. The cross shows us the truth about ourselves.
It also shows the truth about God. Jesus does not answer violence with violence; he answers it with "Father, forgive them." God takes the worst we can do and turns it into the place of mercy.
Paul's point is simple: someone might die for a good person, but Christ died for us "while we were yet sinners." Love that goes this far cannot be earned, only received.

s30.think: The cross is not God punishing an innocent man to calm his anger. It is the Son freely giving himself, out of love for the Father and for us.
s30.journal: How does it feel to be loved "while you were yet a sinner"?
s30.pray: Soul of Christ, sanctify me. Blood of Christ, inebriate me. Within your wounds, hide me.
s30.do: Look at a crucifix for two minutes in silence today.

s30.title: The thief who stole heaven

story.name: The good thief
story.text:
Two criminals were crucified with Jesus. Luke tells us one mocked him: "If thou be Christ, save thyself and us." The other told him to stop. "We receive the due reward of our deeds; but this man hath done no evil." Then he turned his head and said, "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom."

He had no time to be baptized, to go to Mass, or to fix his past. He simply admitted the truth about himself, recognized who Jesus was, and asked. Jesus answered, "This day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Christian tradition later gave him a name, Dismas, and people say he was the first to enter heaven with Christ.

s30.think: It is never too late. The good thief shows that what God asks first is honesty and trust, not a perfect record.
s30.journal: Write your own "Jesus, remember me" in a few honest words.
s30.pray: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.
s30.do: If you will receive Baptism at the Vigil, rest in the fact that all your past will be washed away. If you are already baptized, prepare for Confession before Easter.

s30.title: Behold your mother
s30.think: From the cross Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple, and the disciple to her. The Church has always seen every disciple in that moment, including you.
s30.journal: How will you keep the Triduum (Holy Thursday, Good Friday, the Easter Vigil) holy this year?
s30.pray: Mary, you stood by the cross. Stand by me in these holy days.
s30.do: Plan your Good Friday: it is a day of fasting and abstinence. Keep it quiet; turn off music and screens where you can.

s30.title: Buried and raised with him
s30.class: What do you still want to know about the Easter Vigil? Where to sit, what to wear, what to say, when to come? Write down every practical question too.
s30.think: Baptism is a burial and a rising: you go down into Christ's death and come up into his new life. That is why the Church baptizes at night, in the Easter Vigil, the holiest night of the year.
s30.journal: Write a letter to God for the night of your sacraments.
s30.pray: Risen Lord, I am ready to die to the old and rise with you.
s30.do: Read your questions once more and talk with your sponsor about the Vigil.

s31.title: They kept going
s31.think: After their Baptism the first Christians "were persevering" in four things: the apostles' teaching, community, the breaking of bread and the prayers. The sacraments were a beginning, not a finish line.
s31.journal: What happened in you at Easter? Write down what you remember before it fades.
s31.pray: Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. Pray for me, that I may keep the joy of Easter.
s31.do: Choose one of the four (teaching, community, Eucharist, prayer) to grow in this month.

s31.title: Our hearts were burning
s31.think: This is the road this whole app is named after. Two sad disciples walk away from Jerusalem. A stranger walks with them, explains the Scriptures, and they recognize him in the breaking of the bread. Word and Eucharist: the same pattern as every Mass.
s31.journal: Looking back over your journey, when was Jesus walking beside you before you recognized him?
s31.pray: Stay with us, Lord, for it is evening. Stay with me on every road.

s31.title: Peace be with you

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron's Easter sermons
media.about: In his Sunday sermons for the Easter season, Bishop Barron explains why the resurrection changes everything: if Jesus rose, then death is not the last word, his claims are true, and our lives must be reordered around him. Pick one sermon from the Sundays after Easter.
media.listen: what changes in your life if Jesus really rose.

s31.think: The risen Jesus comes through locked doors to frightened friends and says "Peace be to you." He breathes the Spirit on them. The same Spirit you received now lives in you.
s31.journal: What doors in your life are still locked out of fear?
s31.pray: Risen Jesus, come through my locked doors and give me your peace.
s31.do: Go to Mass this Sunday early and spend five minutes in thanksgiving afterwards.

s31.title: What about the scandals?

reason.q: How can I belong to a Church whose members, even leaders, have done terrible things?
steps: First, the anger is right. Abuse and cover-ups are grave evils, and the victims come first. In Canada this includes the harm done in residential schools; Pope Francis came in 2022 to apologize in person.
Jesus never promised a Church without sinners. In this parable the weeds grow with the wheat until the harvest. One of the twelve apostles betrayed him, and Peter denied him.
The truth of the faith does not depend on the holiness of its ministers. A sick doctor does not make medicine false. The sacraments act through Christ, not through the priest's goodness.
The answer to bad Catholics is not fewer Catholics but holier ones. The saints were often the Church's strongest reformers, from inside.

s31.think: Peter, who denied Jesus three times, was asked three times "Do you love me?" and made shepherd. The Church is a hospital for sinners, and we are all patients.
s31.journal: What disappoints you about the Church, honestly? What keeps you here?
s31.pray: Lord, heal those who were hurt by your Church, and make me part of its healing.
s31.do: Pray for survivors of abuse and for the healing of Indigenous peoples in Canada.

s31.title: At last, God is mine

story.name: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton
story.text:
Elizabeth was born in New York in 1774 and raised in the Episcopal Church. She married a businessman and had five children. Then his business failed and he fell ill. They sailed to Italy hoping the climate would heal him, but he died there, leaving her a widow at twenty-nine.

In Italy a Catholic family cared for her, and she watched them pray before the Blessed Sacrament. She longed to believe that Jesus was truly there. Back home, against the wishes of family and friends, many of whom turned away from her, she became Catholic in 1805. After her first Communion she wrote: "At last, God is mine and I am his." She went on to found a religious order and Catholic schools, and became the first saint born in the United States.

s31.think: Elizabeth paid a price for becoming Catholic, and found it worth it. The Eucharist was the treasure that drew her, and it is now yours too.
s31.journal: What did you feel at your first Communion (or what do you hope to feel)? Write it down.
s31.pray: Jesus, bread of life, at last you are mine and I am yours.
s31.do: Visit a church this week and pray before the tabernacle for a few minutes.

s31.title: Doers of the word
s31.think: James says hearing without doing is like looking in a mirror and forgetting your own face. Mystagogy is learning to live as who you now are: a son or daughter of God.
s31.journal: What daily or weekly habits will keep your faith alive after RCIA ends?
s31.pray: Lord, let me not only hear your word but live it.
s31.do: Set two or three simple weekly habits in the app: Sunday Mass, daily prayer, one act of service.

s31.title: A people set apart
s31.class: What do you want to ask now that you have received the sacraments? What surprised you? What is still unclear?
s31.think: Peter writes to new Christians: "you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation." Once you were not a people; now you are God's people.
s31.journal: How do you feel about being called a neophyte, a "new plant" in the Church?
s31.pray: Thank you, Lord, for calling me out of darkness into your wonderful light.
s31.do: Read your questions once more before class.

s32.title: Tongues of fire
s32.think: At Pentecost the Spirit comes like wind and fire, and frightened disciples go out into the street. People from many nations, including Parthians, Medes and Elamites from the lands of Iran, hear the Gospel in their own languages.
s32.journal: What did you hear in class about being sent? Who comes to mind?
s32.pray: Come, Holy Spirit, fill my heart and set it on fire with your love.
s32.do: Pray the Morning Offering when you wake up, giving your whole day to God.

s32.title: Go and make disciples
s32.think: The last words of Matthew's Gospel are a mission and a promise: go to all nations, baptize, teach, and "behold I am with you all days." Some still doubted, and Jesus sent them anyway.
s32.journal: You do not need to have every answer to share your faith. What part of your story could you share?
s32.pray: Jesus, you are with me all days. Send me where you want me.

s32.title: Every Catholic is a missionary

media.by: Bishop Robert Barron, Word on Fire
media.title: Bishop Barron on evangelization
media.about: Bishop Barron explains that evangelizing is not pushing people; it is sharing something beautiful and true that you have found. He often says to begin with beauty, then goodness, and then truth: let people see a life changed by Christ, and the questions will come.
media.listen: why beauty is often the first door to faith.

s32.think: "How shall they hear without a preacher?" Paul asks. Every one of us came to faith because someone told us. Now it is our turn.
s32.journal: Who first spoke to you about Jesus? What did they do that helped?
s32.pray: Lord, make my life something beautiful that points to you.
s32.do: Thank the person who first spoke to you about Jesus, with a message or a prayer.

s32.title: How do I talk to my family?

reason.q: My family does not share my faith, or even opposes it. What should I say?
steps: Peter says to be ready to give a reason for your hope, but "with modesty and fear": gently and with respect. Winning an argument is not the goal; love is.
Honour your parents and family, even when you disagree. The fourth commandment does not end at Baptism. Often a kinder, more patient you is the strongest argument.
Share your story, not a lecture: what you were looking for, what you found, what changed. People can argue with ideas, but it is hard to argue with your experience.
If speaking openly could put you in danger, your safety comes first. God sees your heart. Pray for your family every day, and talk with your priest about your situation.

s32.think: St. Monica prayed for her son Augustine for seventeen years. Your prayers for your family are never wasted.
s32.journal: Write three sentences that tell the story of your faith, as you might tell a family member.
s32.pray: Lord, bless my family. Let them see your love in me.
s32.do: Do something kind for a family member today, without saying why.

s32.title: The teacher of Ville-Marie

story.name: St. Marguerite Bourgeoys
story.text:
Marguerite was born in Troyes, France, in 1620. At twenty, walking in a procession, she looked at a statue of Mary and felt her heart turned toward God for good. In 1653 she sailed to Ville-Marie, the tiny, struggling settlement that would become Montreal.

In 1658 she opened the first school there, in an old stone stable. She welcomed French and Indigenous children, and later the young women sent from France to settle and marry, teaching them to read, to run a home and to pray. In a time when religious sisters lived behind walls, she founded a community of women who went out among the people, like Mary hurrying to visit Elizabeth. She built the chapel of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours, which still stands in Old Montreal. She was the first woman saint of Canada.

s32.think: Mary, carrying Jesus within her, hurried to serve her cousin, and Elizabeth's child leapt for joy. When we carry Christ, we bring joy to others without needing many words.
s32.journal: Who could you visit or help this week, as Mary visited Elizabeth?
s32.pray: St. Marguerite Bourgeoys, pray for Canada and for all who teach the faith.
s32.do: Find one ministry at your parish where you could help: welcoming, music, youth, the poor, or the next RCIA group.

s32.title: Salt and light
s32.think: Jesus does not say "try to be" salt and light. He says "You are." Your faith is not meant to be hidden under a bushel; it is meant to give flavour and light to the place you live and work.
s32.journal: Where in your daily life could you be a little more salt and light?
s32.pray: Lord, let my light shine so that others may glorify you, not me.
s32.do: Do your work today with honesty and care, as an offering to God.

s32.title: Follow me
s32.class: This is the last class. What do you still want to ask? About next steps, a parish group, a Bible study, being a sponsor one day? Write it down, and write a thank you for your catechists.
s32.think: By the lake, the risen Jesus asks Peter three times, "Do you love me?" and three times gives him a mission: feed my sheep. Then the same words he said at the very beginning: "Follow me." The journey does not end here. It starts again, every day.
s32.journal: Look back at your first journal entry in this app. How has God led you since then?
s32.pray: Lord, you know all things. You know that I love you. I will follow you.
s32.do: Choose your next step: read the whole Bible in a year, join a parish group, or keep your weekly habits.
